title: An archive must choose how to store a collection that may support detailed reanalysis while preserving capacity for future collections whose size is unknown

strategy_1.name: higher fidelity
strategy_1.property_1: Storing this collection requires more space, leaving less capacity for future collections.
strategy_1.property_2: The stored data retains more detail, preserving information that may be useful for later reanalysis.
strategy_1.candidate: I support the strategy with more storage space is required and stored data has higher fidelity.
arguments: Discarding detail closes off some future questions permanently because the original information cannot be recovered.
The current collection fits at higher fidelity. An immediate shortage therefore does not compel the archive to reduce it.
A request for detailed reanalysis may depend on distinctions that a routine summary does not preserve.
Preserving the records leaves their detail available even when a particular user needs only a summary.
Future collections have an unknown size and arrival time. Reserving capacity for them means sacrificing some information already in hand for a demand that has not been established.
An archive may reasonably place special weight on irreversible loss when it cannot yet identify which details later investigators will need.

strategy_2.name: reduced storage
strategy_2.property_1: Storing this collection requires less space, leaving more capacity for future collections.
strategy_2.property_2: The stored data retains less detail, discarding information that may be useful for later reanalysis.
strategy_2.candidate: I support the strategy with less storage space is required and stored data has lower fidelity.
arguments: Space used by this collection is unavailable for future material, and the team cannot assume that more capacity will be supplied.
Not every future request will require detailed reanalysis. Routine summaries may make limited use of the extra fidelity.
The archive has responsibilities beyond the collection currently before it; leaving room for later collections acknowledges those competing demands.
Immediate fit is not the same as adequate future capacity. A policy can satisfy today’s storage constraint while leaving little flexibility for what follows.
Choosing lower fidelity makes the cost explicit: some detail is lost in exchange for additional room. That exchange can be justified without claiming the lost information is worthless.
If later collections are large, spare capacity could matter more than distinctions retained in this one. Their uncertain size keeps that possibility relevant without making it certain.

strategy_1.priority: Your role prioritizes preserving data fidelity over reducing storage use. This priority should inform your assessment throughout the discussion, but you may still maintain or revise your position based on the information available in the scenario and discussion.

strategy_2.priority: Your role prioritizes reducing storage requirements over preserving maximum data fidelity. This priority should inform your assessment throughout the discussion, but you may still maintain or revise your position based on the information available in the scenario and discussion.

candidate_variants: I favor higher data fidelity, accepting greater storage requirements.
I favor lower storage requirements, accepting lower data fidelity.
variant_provenance: Explicitly authored validation-only paraphrases; not used for conversation decisions.
context: The current collection fits under either policy. Future requests may need detailed records or only summaries, but their frequency is unknown. Discarded detail cannot be recovered, and additional capacity cannot be assumed. The team has no agreed weighting of fidelity against storage reduction.
topic: How should an archive balance data fidelity and storage capacity?
